text: For a group \(G\) let \(D_n(G)=G\cap(1+\Delta(G)^n)\) be its integral dimension subgroups and \(\gamma_n(G)\) its lower central series. Whether \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) for every group \(G\) is open (Kourovka Notebook, Problem 20.84); for Lie rings the analogous inclusion was recently proved by Ionin, Mikhailov and Petrov and formally verified in Lean. We reduce the group question, by an elementary argument, to finite metabelian \(2\)-groups of class three, and identify the steps of the Lie-ring proof that have no group-theoretic counterpart. A computer search shows that a counterexample among finite \(2\)-groups of class three has order at least \(2^{12}\). For \(3\)-torsion in \(D_5/\gamma_5\) we prove that \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\) whenever \(G/\gamma_2(G)\) is a finite \(3\)-group with at most one invariant larger than \(3\), and, with the help of a computer search, for all \(3\)-groups of order at most \(3^9\). Along the way we give an exact criterion for a \(p\)-group of type \((d,2,1)\) with elementary abelian \(P/\gamma_2(P)\), \(p\) odd, to have immediate descendants, and an explicit graded Lie algebra of type \((3,3,1,1)\) over \(\mathbb F_p\) with \([L_2,L_2]\ne0\); it shows that the Lie-ring lemma behind our metabelian results requires \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) to have at most two generators.

Conventions on proofs. Results whose proofs depend on computer calculations are labelled or noted as computer-assisted: Propositions 5.1, 5.3 and 5.10, Theorems 5.4 and 6.14, and the first statement of Proposition 5.7. Other computational facts, such as examples, counts and checks, are identified as computations where they occur. All other proofs are by hand: here, in the cited sources, or, where indicated, in the documentation accompanying the code. The computations use GAP [GAP] with the SmallGroups library [BEO02] and the ANUPQ package [GNO], together with our own code; §5 explains why the lattice computations modulo a prime power are exact and how their results were checked by independent implementations. The code, raw tables and checks are available at https://github.com/ispacex/dimension-subrings. Many of the results proved by hand are, in addition, formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib; the formalization is available at https://github.com/ispacex/group-dimension. This is noted at each such result, and §4 states the formal versions with their exact hypotheses. For the \(3400\) groups of Proposition 5.3 the formalization also contains certificates of \(D_5=1\), checked with native_decide.

Let \(\Delta=\Delta(G)\) be the augmentation ideal of \(\mathbb{Z}[G]\) and \(D_n(G)=\{g\in G: g-1\in\Delta^n\}\). Always \(\gamma_n(G)\subseteq D_n(G)\) (this is also formally verified, §4), with equality for \(n\le 3\) and failure for \(n=4\) in general (Rips [Rip72]).
Question ( [KM26, Problem 20.84], [IMP26, §1.3]). Is \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) for every group \(G\)?

Known facts used below, all from the cited sources (the first one is also formally verified, see §4): \(D_4(G)^2\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) (Passi [Pas68], see also [MP09]); \(D_n(G)/\gamma_n(G)\) is abelian [GK92]; the exponent of \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) divides \(3!=6\) (Tahara [Tah81, Cor. 6.11], proved there for finite groups, to which the general case reduces by the standard argument; Tahara also gives an explicit description of \(D_5\) for finite groups of class \(4\) [Tah81, Thm. 6.1] and shows \(D_k=\gamma_k\) for \(k\le5\) when \(G\) has no elements of order \(2\) or \(3\) [Tah81, Cor. 6.12]); Gupta's claim that all \(D_n/\gamma_n\) are \(2\)-groups [Gup02] is false: Bartholdi and Mikhailov constructed a \(3\)-group with \(D_7\neq\gamma_7\) [BM23].

Related work. For metabelian groups much more is known. Gupta proved \(D_n(G)=\gamma_n(G)\) for \(n\le2p-1\) in metabelian \(p\)-groups [Gup88], and that for a finite metabelian group \(G\) the exponent of \(D_n(G)/\gamma_n(G)\) is a power of \(2\); in particular \(D_n=\gamma_n\) for all \(n\) in finitely generated metabelian \(p\)-groups with \(p\) odd [Gup91]. This result is taken as proved in [BM23, §1.1], unlike his later claims for all groups [Gup02]. Sjogren bounded the exponent of \(D_n(G)/\gamma_n(G)\) by a function of \(n\) alone [Sjo79]. Question 1.1 is also Problem 16.66(a) of [KM26] (Mikhailov and Passi): it asks for \(f(3)\), the largest \(m\) with \(D_m(G)\ne1\) for some nilpotent group \(G\) of class \(3\), and by Rips's example the question is whether \(f(3)=4\). Examples of \(2\)-groups of class \(3\) with \(D_4\ne1\) and \(D_5=1\) are in [SGu16]; conditions under which \(D_5=\gamma_5\) for certain finite \(2\)-groups (of class \(3\) in [GK23]) and \(3\)-groups, derived from Tahara's Theorem 6.1, are in [GK19,GK21,GK23]. We have not verified the arguments of [SGu16,GK19,GK21,GK23], and do not use their results.

Results and plan of the paper. Section 2 reduces Question 1.1 to finite metabelian \(2\)-groups of class exactly \(3\) (Proposition 2.1). Section 3 summarises the proof of the Lie-ring analogue in [IMP26] and lists the steps that have no counterpart for groups; Section 4 describes the Lean formalization. Section 5 reports the computations: \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of class \(3\) and order \(2^{10}\) or \(2^{11}\) (Propositions 5.3 and 5.10), so that a counterexample among finite \(2\)-groups of class \(3\) has order at least \(2^{12}\), together with consequences for finite groups of small order (Theorem 5.4). Section 6 treats \(3\)-torsion in \(D_5/\gamma_5\): \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\) whenever \(G/\gamma_2(G)\) is a finite \(3\)-group with at most one invariant larger than \(3\) (Theorems 6.6 and 6.8), and for every \(3\)-group of order at most \(3^9\) (Theorem 6.14); on the way it proves the criterion for immediate descendants of Theorem 6.12. Section 7 collects open questions. Appendix A gives the Lie algebra of type \((3,3,1,1)\), and Appendices B and C contain the longer proofs.

Proposition. The following are equivalent. • \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) for every group \(G\). • \(D_5(M)=1\) for every metabelian group \(M\) of nilpotency class at most \(3\). • \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every finite metabelian \(2\)-group \(Q\) of nilpotency class exactly \(3\).

Proof. (The proposition is also formally verified, without hypotheses, since Passi's and Gruenberg's theorems and \(D_3=\gamma_3\) are formalized too, and with “metabelian” dropped by Remark 2.2; see §4.)
\((1)\Rightarrow(3)\) is clear since \(\gamma_4(Q)=1\).

\((2)\Rightarrow(1)\). Put \(N=\gamma_4(G)G''\). Since \(G''=[\gamma_2(G),\gamma_2(G)]\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\), \(N=\gamma_4(G)\), and \(M=G/N\) is metabelian of class \(\le 3\). The projection \(\pi\colon G\to M\) induces a ring map \(\mathbb{Z}[G]\to\mathbb{Z}[M]\) sending \(\Delta(G)^n\) into \(\Delta(M)^n\), so \(\pi(D_5(G))\subseteq D_5(M)=1\), i.e. \(D_5(G)\subseteq N=\gamma_4(G)\). (This is the group version of the step from Theorem C to Corollary D in [IMP26].)

\((3)\Rightarrow(2)\). Let \(M\) be metabelian of class \(\le3\) and \(1\ne x\in D_5(M)\). Finite generation. \(x-1\) is a finite \(\mathbb{Z}\)-linear combination of products \((g_1-1)\cdots(g_5-1)\); all \(g_i\) and \(x\) lie in a finitely generated subgroup \(H\), and then \(x\in D_5(H)\). \(H\) is metabelian of class \(\le 3\), hence finitely generated nilpotent. Exponent two. By Passi, \(D_4(H)^2\subseteq\gamma_4(H)=1\); as \(D_5\subseteq D_4\), \(x^2=1\). Finite \(2\)-quotients. Let \(T\) be the (finite, normal) subgroup of elements of odd order of \(H\); \(x\notin T\). The group \(H/T\) is finitely generated nilpotent with \(2\)-group torsion, hence residually a finite \(2\)-group (Gruenberg [Gru57]). Choose a finite \(2\)-group quotient \(Q\) of \(H\) in which the image of \(x\) is nontrivial; by functoriality it lies in \(D_5(Q)\). \(Q\) is metabelian of class \(\le 3\), and class \(\le 2\) is impossible because then \(D_5(Q)\subseteq D_3(Q)=\gamma_3(Q)=1\).

Remark (“metabelian” is automatic). Every group of nilpotency class \(\le 3\) is metabelian: \(G''=[\gamma_2(G),\gamma_2(G)]\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) by P. Hall's inclusion \([\gamma_i,\gamma_j]\subseteq\gamma_{i+j}\) (see e.g. [MP09]); this is the same fact used in \((2)\Rightarrow(1)\). So in (2) and (3) the word “metabelian” may be dropped: (3) is the statement that \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every finite \(2\)-group of class \(3\), and the search space of §5 is simply the \(2\)-groups of class \(3\). The same holds for Lie rings (\([\gamma_2,\gamma_2]\subseteq\gamma_4\)), so Theorem C of [IMP26] for \(c=3\) needs no metabelian hypothesis either; the hypothesis matters only for \(c\ge4\), where \(D_{2c-1}=1\) for all groups of class \(\le c\) is a different, stronger question. Accordingly, ANUPQ's option Metabelian cut nothing in our searches. That groups of class \(\le3\) are metabelian is also formally verified (§4).

Remark (a bounded form). For finite groups the proof gives more. If \(G\) is finite then so are \(M=G/\gamma_4(G)\) and \(H\le M\), and one may take \(Q=H/T\), a finite \(2\)-group whose order is the \(2\)-part of \(|H|\), hence divides the \(2\)-part of \(|G|\). Therefore: if \(D_5(Q)=1\) for all metabelian \(2\)-groups \(Q\) of class \(3\) and order \(\le 2^k\), then \(D_5(G)\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\) for every finite group \(G\) whose Sylow \(2\)-subgroup has order \(\le 2^k\). This is also formally verified (§4), without hypotheses and both for \(Q\) of class \(\le3\) and of class exactly \(3\), since Passi's theorem and \(D_3=\gamma_3\) are formalized; the formal proof does not need Gruenberg's theorem, as there \(H=M\) and \(Q\) is the Sylow \(2\)-subgroup of \(M\), a direct factor since \(M\) is nilpotent. Note that the exponent step uses Passi's theorem for \(H\) (where \(\gamma_4(H)=1\)), not for an arbitrary group.

Remark. Proposition 2.1(2) is precisely the group analogue of Theorem C of [IMP26] for \(c=3\) (“a metabelian Lie ring of class \(\le c\) has \(D_{2c-1}=0\)”). The reduction is elementary and almost certainly known to experts; we record it because it fixes the search space for computations (§5).

We summarise the proof of [IMP26, Theorem C, Corollary D], checked against its text; the final statements are formally verified in the Lean formalization accompanying [IMP26]. • Reduction to \(L\) metabelian of class \(\le c\) (Corollary 6.14) and to finitely generated \(L\) (Lemma 6.13). Transfers: this is Proposition 2.1. • A central extension \(0\to K\to T\to L\to0\), \(T=L\times_{L_{ab}}P\) with \(P\) free abelian, such that \(\gamma_i(T)\cong\gamma_i(L)\) for \(i\ge2\) and \(T\cong T'\oplus P\) additively (Lemma 6.4, Corollary 6.7). • The integral PBW theorem: \(\mathrm{gr}\,U(T)\cong\mathrm{Sym}_\mathbb{Z}(T)\) and, for \(T\) a direct sum of cyclic groups, an explicit \(\mathbb{Z}\)-basis of ordered monomials with known additive orders (Theorem 2.3, Corollary 2.4). • The additive projection \(p\colon U(T)\to P_{\le2}U(T)\) onto monomials of length \(\le 2\) (§6.2), and a retraction \(r\colon P_{\le2}U(T)\to T\) killing \(Z(T)\cdot T\) (Lemma 5.3). • The quadratic part of \(p(\varpi(T)^n)\) lies in \(\sum_{i+j=n}\gamma_i(T)\gamma_j(T)\) (Proposition 6.12); for \(n=2c-1\) every such term has a central factor, and Theorem 5.1 gives \(D_{2c-1}(L)=0\).
section: 3. The Lie-ring proof and where it does not transfer

text: Obstacles for groups. The following is our analysis; where no source is cited, it is an explanation, not a theorem. • No PBW basis of the required kind. Step 3 is the heart of the argument: it gives an additive splitting of \(U(T)\) by monomial length, compatible with additive orders, so that “the quadratic part” of an element is well defined and computable. For \(\mathbb{Z}[G]\) the filtration by powers of \(\Delta\) has associated graded ring \(\bigoplus\Delta^n/\Delta^{n+1}\), which in general is not the integral enveloping algebra of \(\mathrm{gr}\,\gamma_\bullet(G)\); over \(\mathbb Q\) the analogous comparison is Quillen's theorem [Qui68], and over \(\mathbb{Z}\) its failure is essentially the dimension subgroup problem itself (cf. [HMP07,MP09]). There is no canonical additive projection of \(\mathbb{Z}[G]\) onto “length \(\le 2\)”. • The extension \(T\). Step 2 has a formal group analogue (pull back a free abelian cover of \(G_{ab}\) along \(G\to G_{ab}\), giving a central extension with the same higher lower central terms). What is missing is how to use it: in the Lie case \(T'\) is an additive direct summand and its elements commute in \(U(T)\), which drives the rewriting Lemmas 6.9–6.10. In \(\mathbb{Z}[G]\) products of commutators do not commute and the corresponding rewriting produces higher-order terms (“collection”). • Torsion is already there in degree four. For Lie rings \(D_n=\gamma_n\) for \(n\le3\) and \(2D_4\subseteq\gamma_4\) [BP15], the same pattern as for groups; but for groups even the description of \(D_4/\gamma_4\) requires the full Rips–Passi machinery, and the known group computations of \(D_5\) (e.g. the group of [IMP26, §3.3], where \(D_5(G)=\langle w\rangle\subseteq\gamma_4(G)\)) are case-by-case.

Method. For finite \(G\), \(\Delta\) is free abelian with basis \(\{g-1\}_{g
e1}\), and \(\Delta^n=\mathrm{span}_\mathbb{Z}\{b(x_i-1): b 	ext{ in a basis of } \Delta^{n-1},\ x_i 	ext{ generators}\}\): no closure under further multiplication is needed, since \(\Delta\) is the left ideal generated by the \(x_i-1\) and \(\Delta^{n-1}\mathbb{Z}[G]=\Delta^{n-1}\). The lattices are computed in Howell form over \(\mathbb{Z}/p^E\) (\(E=30,19,13\) for \(p=2,3,5\)), which is exact for our purpose: \(g-1
otin\Delta^n+p^E\Delta\) implies \(g-1
otin\Delta^n\), and the equalities \(D_n=\gamma_n\) below are proved by such non-memberships (memberships are certified separately by \(p^{E-1}\Delta\subseteq\Delta^n+p^E\Delta\)). Groups are taken from the SmallGroups library [BEO02] of GAP [GAP]; each group is computed until \(D_n=1\).

Sieves (theorems, used to skip groups): \(p\)-class \(\ge\) class, so groups of \(p\)-class \(2\) have class \(\le2\); for \(2\)-groups of class \(3\), \(D_5\subseteq D_3=\gamma_3\), Jennings' theorem \(D_n\subseteq M_n\) (the mod-\(2\) dimension subgroups) and Passi's \(D_4^2\subseteq\gamma_4=1\) give \(D_5\subseteq\Omega_1(\gamma_3\cap M_5)\), so only groups with \(K=\Omega_1(\gamma_3\cap M_5)\ne1\) need the lattice; for \(3\)-groups of class \(4\) the analogous \(K=\Omega_1(\gamma_4\cap M_5)\), using \(D_4=\gamma_4\) for groups without \(2\)-torsion (from Passi's \(D_4^2\subseteq\gamma_4\) [Pas68]) and Tahara's bound \(D_5^6\subseteq\gamma_5\) [Tah81, Cor. 6.11].

This order is not in SmallGroups, and generating all \(2\)-groups of class \(3\) of this order is out of reach: at rank \(\ge4\) the \(p\)-group generation tree has millions of nodes already at order \(2^9\). Notation. \(P_1(Q)=Q\), \(P_{i+1}(Q)=[P_i(Q),Q]\,P_i(Q)^2\) is the lower exponent-\(2\) central series, and the \(2\)-class of \(Q\) is the least \(c\) with \(P_{c+1}(Q)=1\); \(M_n(Q)=Q\cap(1+\Delta_{\mathbb F_2}(Q)^n)\) are the mod-\(2\) dimension subgroups, \(M_n=\prod_{i2^j\ge n}\gamma_i^{2^j}\) (Jennings [Jen41], Lazard [Laz54]). If \(Q\) has \(2\)-class \(c\ge2\), it is an immediate descendant of \(Q/P_c(Q)\) of step size \(\log_2|P_c(Q)|\); the \(p\)-group generation algorithm [OBr90], as implemented in ANUPQ [GNO], lists all immediate descendants of a given group of a given step size, up to isomorphism.

Lemma (minimal counterexample). Let \(Q\) be a finite \(2\)-group of class \(3\) such that \(D_5(Q/N)=1\) for every central subgroup \(N\) of order \(2\). If \(D_5(Q)\ne1\), then (a) \(Z(Q)\) is cyclic and \(D_5(Q)=\Omega_1(Z(Q))=\langle n\rangle\) has order \(2\); (b) \(n\in\gamma_3(Q)\cap M_5(Q)\); (c) the \(2\)-class \(c\) of \(Q\) is at least \(4\), and \(P_c(Q)=\langle n\rangle\); (d) \(Q\) is an immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(R=Q/\langle n\rangle\), a group of class \(2\) or \(3\) and \(2\)-class \(c-1\ge3\) with \(\gamma_3(R)\) cyclic.
Proof. (The lemma is also formally verified, §4.)

(a) Let \(N\le Z(Q)\), \(|N|=2\). The projection \(Q\to Q/N\) maps \(D_5(Q)\) into \(D_5(Q/N)=1\), so \(D_5(Q)\subseteq N\). Hence a nontrivial \(D_5(Q)\) equals every central subgroup of order \(2\): there is only one, so \(\Omega_1(Z(Q))\) has order \(2\), the abelian \(2\)-group \(Z(Q)\) is cyclic, and \(D_5(Q)=\Omega_1(Z(Q))\). (b) \(D_5\subseteq D_3=\gamma_3\), and \(D_5(Q)\subseteq M_5(Q)\) because \(\mathbb{Z}[Q]\to\mathbb F_2[Q]\) maps \(\Delta^5\) into \(\Delta_{\mathbb F_2}^5\). (c) Since \(\gamma_i\subseteq P_i\) and \(P_i^2\subseteq P_{i+1}\), we have \(\gamma_i^{2^j}\subseteq P_{i+j}\), and \(i2^j\ge5\) implies \(i+j\ge4\). So \(M_5\subseteq P_4\), and \(1\ne n\in P_4(Q)\) gives \(c\ge4\). The subgroup \(P_c(Q)\) is nontrivial, central and elementary abelian, hence equal to \(\Omega_1(Z(Q))=\langle n\rangle\). (d) By (c), \(R=Q/P_c(Q)\), the step size is \(1\) and \(R\) has \(2\)-class \(c-1\ge3\). \(R\) has class \(\le3\); if \(R\) were abelian, then \(\gamma_2(Q)\subseteq\langle n\rangle\subseteq Z(Q)\) and \(Q\) would have class \(\le2\). Finally \(\gamma_3(R)\) is a quotient of \(\gamma_3(Q)\subseteq Z(Q)\), which is cyclic.
Proposition (Computer-assisted). \(D_5(Q)=1\) for every \(2\)-group \(Q\) of order \(2^{10}\) and class \(3\) (all of them are metabelian, Remark 2.2).

Proof. Let \(Q\) be such a group with \(D_5(Q)\ne1\). For every central \(N\) of order \(2\) the quotient \(Q/N\) has order \(2^9\) and class \(\le3\), so \(D_5(Q/N)=1\): by Proposition 5.1 for class \(3\), and since \(D_5\subseteq D_3=\gamma_3=1\) for class \(\le2\). By Lemma 5.2, \(Q\) is then isomorphic to an immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of a group \(R\) of order \(2^9\), of class \(2\) or \(3\) and \(2\)-class \(\ge3\), with \(\gamma_3(R)\) cyclic, and \(Q\) has class \(3\), cyclic centre, and its involution \(n\) of the centre lies in \(\gamma_3(Q)\cap M_5(Q)\). From here on the argument is computational. The SmallGroups library contains \(1\,422\,862\) such groups \(R\). For each, ANUPQ (GAP 4.15.1 [GAP], ANUPQ 3.3.2 [GNO]) lists the immediate descendants of step size \(1\) up to isomorphism, \(1\,819\,675\) groups in all; \(88\,809\) of them have class \(3\), and exactly \(3400\) of these have cyclic centre with involution in \(\gamma_3\cap M_5\) (by rank \(d(Q)=2,3,4,5,6\): \(15\), \(301\), \(2756\), \(319\), \(9\); none of rank \(7\)). For each of the \(3400\) the lattice computation of §5 gives \(D_4(Q)=D_5(Q)=1\), in fact \(D_n(Q)=\gamma_n(Q)\) for all \(n\). This contradicts \(D_5(Q)\ne1\).
